terms.comment: Properly the gullet (Cic. N.D. 2.135), then, commonly, the stomach. It also means taste, liking (lūdī nōn tuī stomachī, Cic. Fam. 7.1.2) and, often in Cicero’s letters, irritation (see be-cross). “To have stomach trouble” is stomachō labōrāre (Traupman 66).
The belly as a whole, and the stomach as what is full or empty (see belly).
Diminutive of venter; the medical writers’ word for the stomach; ventriculus cordis is a ventricle of the heart (Cic. N.D. 2.138).

phrases.latin: cum sale pānis lātrantem stomachum bene lēniet
phrases.english: bread with salt will soothe a growling stomach nicely
tasting lots of things is the mark of a fussy stomach

phrases.latin: ōrātiōnem Graecam Latīnamve clārē et intentē nōn tam vōcis causā quam stomachī legō
phrases.english: I read a speech in Greek or Latin loudly and with effort, not so much for my voice as for my digestion
